bibliography.abstract: Fabric retrofit is central to decarbonising housing, and planning it depends on expected savings and their uncertainty. This study asks which upgrade saves most per dwelling and across a housing portfolio, how uncertain the savings are, and whether upgrade order matters. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that converts predicted changes in energy performance certificate scores after wall, roof and window upgrades into standardised energy-cost savings and emission reductions. Six machine-learning models predict the 1-100 Standard Assessment Procedure (SAP) energy-cost and environmental impact (EI) emission scores from 17 certificate descriptors. Each model's errors on similar dwellings give calibrated prediction intervals. A global-best strategy applies the most accurate model throughout; a sample-specific strategy chooses each dwelling's model using these local errors. The analysis covers 103,414 officially registered dwellings in Westminster, London. CatBoost was the global-best model, with mean absolute errors of 3.487 SAP and 4.379 EI points on held-out dwellings. Both strategies projected similar savings; under global-best, roof insulation saved most per dwelling, GBP 203 annually (uncertainty range 176-229), and wall insulation most across the portfolio, GBP 6.09 million annually (uncertainty range 5.69-6.72). For 5,382 dwellings needing all three upgrades, every order delivered the same final package, yet installing roofs, walls, then windows a year apart accumulated 54% more projected cost savings over three years than the reverse order. Emission reductions followed the same pattern. Using only certificate data, the framework helps local authorities rank measures for dwellings and portfolios and sequence upgrades to bring savings forward.
bibliography.title: Fabric retrofit scenario analysis under uncertainty for an urban housing stock using machine learning

en.caveats: The performance predictions and economic savings rely exclusively on administrative Energy Performance Certificate descriptors rather than direct, in-situ energy metering.
en.what: The authors developed an uncertainty-aware framework using CatBoost to predict Standard Assessment Procedure (SAP) energy-cost and emission scores from 17 Energy Performance Certificate descriptors across 103,414 dwellings in Westminster, London. CatBoost achieved mean absolute errors of 3.487 SAP and 4.379 Environmental Impact points, finding that roof insulation yields the highest per-dwelling savings at £203 annually (176–229 range), while wall insulation saves the most portfolio-wide at £6.09 million annually (5.69–6.72 million range). For dwellings requiring three full retrofits, sequencing roof, wall, then window upgrades a year apart accumulated 54% more cost savings over three years compared to the reverse order.
en.why: This approach quantifies the compounding financial benefits of retrofit ordering, proving that upgrade sequencing significantly affects short-term cumulative savings even when the final building package remains identical.
